paper_description: This paper introduces a novel strong Hierarchical Processor Affinity (HPA) scheduler that significantly improves runtime complexity compared to previous arbitrary processor affinity (APA) schedulers. It provides theoretical guarantees for schedulability under HPA and demonstrates its practical viability through an implementation and benchmarking. The core contribution is an efficient algorithm for strong APA scheduling in the HPA context, enabling better schedulability analysis and practical implementation.

formal_description.statement: At the end of Algorithm 1 there exists a matching in G(t) of all the tasks in τ to processors in π.

variables.τ: set of admitted tasks at time t
variables.G(t): bipartite graph representing task-processor affinities at time t
variables.τ(t): set of ready tasks at time t

assumptions: The family of affinity masks is hierarchical (laminar).
Algorithm 1 has been executed on the set of ready tasks τ(t).
formal_description.conclusion: A matching exists in G(t) that assigns all tasks in the admitted set τ to processors in π, respecting their affinity masks.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma leverages Hall's Marriage Theorem to prove that if the conditions derived from the hierarchical affinity structure are met, then it's always possible to assign the selected tasks to processors without violating their affinity constraints.
steps: The proof relies on showing that for any subset S of the admitted tasks τ, the set of processors reachable by tasks in S (Γ(S)) is at least as large as the size of S. This is the condition required by Hall's Theorem.
The hierarchical structure of affinity masks is crucial. The union of affinity masks for tasks in S can be decomposed into disjoint representative affinity masks.
By bounding the size of the union of these disjoint masks and relating it back to the tasks in S, the condition |Γ(S)| ≥ |S| is established, thus guaranteeing the existence of a matching.
key_insights: Hall's condition (|Γ(S)| ≥ |S|) is the key to proving the existence of a matching.
The laminar property of affinity masks simplifies the analysis of the union of processor sets.
The admission algorithm (Algorithm 1) is designed to ensure Hall's condition is met for the admitted task set τ.

formal_description.statement: For each task T i ∈ τ (t) \ τ , R i (t) = α i .

variables.T i: a task not admitted to be scheduled (T i ∈ τ(t) \ τ)
variables.τ: set of admitted tasks at time t
variables.τ(t): set of ready tasks at time t
variables.R i(t): set of processors reachable from T i in G(t) with respect to the matching χ(t)
variables.α i: affinity mask of task T i

assumptions: T i is a task that was not admitted by Algorithm 1 (i.e., T i ∈ τ(t) \ τ).
α i is the inclusion-wise minimal affinity mask satisfying specific properties related to processor assignments within α i and its supersets.
formal_description.conclusion: The set of processors reachable from an unadmitted task T i is exactly its own affinity mask α i.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma establishes that for tasks that are not admitted for scheduling, the set of processors they can potentially reach (through alternating paths) is precisely their own allowed processor set. This is crucial for proving the strong APA invariant.
steps: The proof shows two parts: (i) there are no alternating paths from T i to any processor outside its affinity mask α i, and (ii) there exists an alternating path from T i to any processor within its affinity mask α i.

Part (i) is proven by contradiction: if an alternating path existed to a processor outside α i, it would imply a contradiction with the definition of α i (specifically, condition 2 regarding processor assignments within α i and its supersets).
Part (ii) is also proven by contradiction: if a processor within α i were not reachable, it would contradict the minimality of α i as defined in Algorithm 2.
key_insights: The definition of α i (the minimal affinity mask for unadmitted tasks) is key to bounding the reachable processors.
The proof relies on the properties of alternating paths in the bipartite graph G(t).
This lemma directly connects the structure of the assignment (χ(t)) to the reachability of processors for tasks that are not scheduled.

formal_description.statement: The matching produced by Algorithm 2 satisfies the Strong Invariant.

variables.τ(t): set of ready tasks at time t

formal_description.conclusion: For any ready task T b not matched by χ(t), and for any processor Π reachable from T b (i.e., Π ∈ R b (t)), there exists a task T i such that (T i , Π) ∈ χ(t) and φ i ≥ φ b.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem is the main result of Section III-B, proving that the proposed assignment algorithm (Algorithm 2) correctly implements strong APA scheduling for hierarchical affinities. It shows that if a task is not scheduled, any processor it could potentially reach is either occupied by a higher-priority task or is part of a structure that ensures higher-priority tasks are prioritized.
steps: The proof breaks down into two parts: (i) showing that for any unadmitted task T i, any task T k matched to a processor in α i has a higher priority (φ k > φ i), and (ii) showing that no processor in α i is idle for any unadmitted task T i.

Part (i) is proven by induction on the iterations of Algorithm 1 (which determines the admitted set τ). It shows that as affinity masks are processed, tasks are only kept if they have higher priorities than those being removed.

Part (ii) is also proven by induction, demonstrating that the admission and assignment algorithms ensure that processors within the relevant affinity masks are utilized by higher-priority tasks, preventing idle processors that could be used by lower-priority tasks.
key_insights: The proof relies on the inductive structure of Algorithm 1 and the properties established by Lemma III.2.
The priority ordering is critical for satisfying the strong invariant.

The algorithm's bottom-up assignment strategy ensures that higher-priority tasks are considered first within their affinity masks, leaving room for lower-priority tasks only if higher-priority ones are satisfied.

formal_description.statement: At any point in time, at least as much total work has been processed in S ∞ as in any schedule which is feasible upon platform π with unit-speed processors and subject to the affinity mask constraints α.

variables.τ 0: set of tasks with global affinity masks
variables.τ i: set of tasks with specific affinity masks (i > 0)
variables.m max: maximum number of processors in any π i (for i > 0)
variables.s: speed of processors in S ∞ (2 -1/m max )

assumptions: A collection of jobs J is feasible on m unit-speed processors under affinity mask constraints α.
The idealized algorithm A ∞ schedules jobs of τ 0 on additional processors with speed s, and jobs of τ i (i > 0) on processors in π i with speed s.
formal_description.conclusion: The idealized schedule S ∞ provides at least as much service to jobs as any feasible schedule on unit-speed processors with the same affinity constraints.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma establishes a baseline for the performance of the idealized scheduler. It states that the idealized scheduler, which uses extra processors and higher speeds for certain tasks, is at least as good as any feasible schedule on the original platform. This is a crucial step in relating the idealized schedule to the actual HPA-EDF scheduler.
steps: The proof compares the work processed by S ∞ and any feasible schedule at any given time.
For tasks in τ 0 (global affinity), S ∞ uses dedicated processors with speed s, which is inherently at least as good as any unit-speed processor assignment.

For tasks in τ i (i > 0), S ∞ uses processors in π i with speed s. The lemma leverages a known result (Lemma 2.6 in [31]) which states that a work-conserving schedule on m i speed-(2 -1/m i ) processors processes at least as much work as any unit-speed schedule on m i processors. Since s = 2 -1/m max and m i ≤ m max, the speed s is sufficient to match or exceed the service provided by a unit-speed schedule.
By combining these observations, S ∞ is shown to provide at least as much work as any feasible schedule.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
Idealized Algorithm A ∞:
1) For each i = 1, . . . , M, schedule jobs of τ i on π i using global EDF with speed s.
2) Allocate one processor Π k (k > m) to each job of τ 0 and schedule them as early as possible with speed s.
key_insights: The idealized schedule uses extra resources (processors and speed) to guarantee a certain level of service.
The proof relies on comparing the service provided by S ∞ to that of any feasible schedule, leveraging known results about processor speedup.
The separation of tasks into global (τ 0) and specific (τ i) affinities is key to the analysis.

formal_description.statement:
Consider a collection J of jobs generated by τ and let s ≥ s . Then at least one of the following holds:
1) All jobs in J are completed within their deadline under HPA-EDF on m processors of speed s, or
2) J is not feasible under the speed-s schedule S ∞ , or
3) there exists an interval I such that any feasible schedule for J must finish more than sm -2(m -1) ss s+s |I| units of work within I.

variables.m i: number of processors in π i
variables.HPA-EDF: Hierarchical Processor Affinities - Earliest Deadline First scheduler

assumptions: The affinity hierarchy is bilevel or clustered.
Jobs are prioritized by Earliest Deadline First (EDF).
formal_description.conclusion: If HPA-EDF with speed s fails to schedule a job collection J that is feasible under the idealized S ∞ with speed s, then there must be a significant 'bottleneck' in any feasible schedule for J, implying a fundamental unschedulability condition.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma is a core part of the speedup analysis. It states that if HPA-EDF (with a certain speed) fails to schedule a job set that *could* be scheduled by an idealized system (with a potentially higher speed), then there must be a fundamental limitation in the system that prevents any schedule from being feasible. This limitation is quantified by the amount of work that any feasible schedule must perform in a specific interval.
steps: The proof uses a proof by contradiction. It assumes that HPA-EDF with speed s fails, but J is feasible under S ∞ with speed s, and no such 'bottleneck' interval I exists.

It defines t* as the latest time where HPA-EDF and S ∞ have processed the same amount of work for all available jobs. The interval of interest is I = [t*, D j ], where D j is the deadline of a job that fails under HPA-EDF.
The interval I is partitioned into sub-intervals (X k, Y k, Z k, W k) based on processor utilization and task types (τ 0 vs. τ i).
Through a series of 'Facts' (which are assumed to be proven elsewhere, e.g., in an extended technical report), the lemma analyzes the amount of work processed by HPA-EDF and S ∞ in these intervals.
The core argument is that if HPA-EDF fails and S ∞ succeeds, the difference in work processed must be attributable to a fundamental system bottleneck, which is captured by the third condition.

Not directly applicable as it's a proof structure, but the core idea involves analyzing work done in intervals:
Analyze work done by HPA-EDF vs. S ∞ in intervals [t*, D j ] partitioned into X k, Y k, Z k, W k.
Use 'Facts' about processor utilization and work processing to derive bounds.
If HPA-EDF fails and S ∞ succeeds, and no bottleneck exists, a contradiction is reached.
key_insights: The lemma establishes a relationship between the performance of HPA-EDF and an idealized scheduler, mediated by processor speed.
The proof relies on a detailed analysis of work done over time intervals, considering different task types and processor availability.
The third condition quantifies a fundamental limitation in the system's schedulability, independent of the specific scheduler (as long as it's work-conserving and respects affinities).
